newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Commodities win from Australian dollar fall.
newsitem.headline: Commodities win from Australian dollar fall.

text.p: Australian commodities exporters are reaping billions of dollars in windfall profits from the falling Australian dollar, which has dropped by almost 10 percent since its recent peak last December.
Gains are being recorded across Australia's A$60 billion commodities export sector, with biggest currency profits scored in coal, iron ore, metals, wool, wheat, sugar and meat.
Almost all of Australia's rural and mineral exports are set in U.S. dollars, producing direct windfall gains for producers.
Peter Walsh, assistant director of the Wool Council of Australia, said that since August 1996 the Australian dollar and the A$3.7 billion wool export market had moved inversely.

Every one cent fall in the Australian dollar against the U.S. dollar in general caused a 15 point change in wool's key Eastern Market Indicator (EMI) price, or a A$70 million to A$80 million gain, he said.

The Australian dollar's drop to about US$0.75 from US$0.82 since December would indicate a 105 point rise in the EMI, he said. Its actual rise this year had been to 755 cents a kg clean from 600 cents.

Australia's A$3.0 billion a year meat exports are also winning from the dollar's fall. Australian Meat and Livestock Corp economist Richard Koch said the Australian dollar's 1997 fall would be worth an extra A$500 million for meat.
Wheat, Australia's biggest rural product with exports worth an estimated A$4.2 billion in 1996/97, would benefit through most of its contracts being set in U.S. dollars, analysts said.

The New South Wales Farmers Federation estimates a A$356 million revenue gain for Australia's A$20 billion farm export sector from every one cent fall in the Australian dollar, based on the trade weighted index.
This indicates gains of some A$3 billion a year in extra returns from the currency's fall so far this year.
Australia's A$35 billion minerals export sector, which almost entirely sells product internationally priced in U.S. dollars, is on a similar currency roll.
Coal, Australia's top traded commodity with forecast 1997 exports of about A$8 billion, gets an extra A$100 million revenue for every one cent fall in the Australian dollar.

The annual A$1 billion windfall gain indicated by the Australian dollar's decline will compensate coal producers for tough pricing deals with Japan this year, in which prices were either steady or slightly decreased.
Like coal, iron ore, a A$3 billion export sold mainly to the Japanese steel mills, is priced in U.S. dollars. Currency gains will offset similarly tough terms with Japan for 1997.
"They will be breathing a lot easier now," Denis Porter, assistant director New South Wales Minerals Council, said.

With gold, copper and Australia's other main metals exports priced in U.S. dollars, the Australian dollar's fall would be producing an overall A$4.0-A$5.0 billion gain for the industry on an annual basis, industry estimates show.
"Primary producers are dancing in the streets," a senior official with Australia's Department of Primary Industries said.
